verses.15:6: Now on the feast day he was accustomed to release to them one of the prisoners, whomever they requested.
verses.15:7: Now there was one called Barabbas, who was bound along with the insurgents and who had committed murder in the insurrection.
verses.15:8: And when the crowd had gone up, they began to ask, just as he always did for them.
verses.15:9: But Pilate answered them and said, "Do you want me to release the King of the Jews to you?"
verses.15:10: For he knew that the chief priests had handed Him over through envy.
verses.15:11: But the high priests incited the crowd so that he would rather release Barabbas to them.
verses.15:12: And Pilate, answering again, said to them, "What then do you want me to do to the King of the Jews?"
verses.15:14: Yet Pilate was saying to them, "Why, what evil did He do?" But they kept shouting all the more, "Crucify Him!"
verses.15:15: Now Pilate, wishing to satisfy the people, released Barabbas to them, and handed over Jesus, scourged with whips, to be crucified.
verses.15:16: Then the soldiers led Him into the courtyard of the praetorium and called together the entire cohort,
verses.15:17: and clothed Him in purple, and weaving a crown of thorns, they placed it upon Him.
verses.15:18: And they began to salute Him, "Hail, King of the Jews!"
verses.15:19: And they kept striking His head with a reed and spitting on Him, and kneeling down, they were worshiping Him.
verses.15:20: And after they had mocked Him, they stripped Him of the purple and clothed Him in His own garments; and they led Him out to crucify Him.
verses.15:21: And they forced a certain man passing by into service, Simon the Cyrenian, coming from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus, so that he might carry His cross.
verses.15:22: And they brought Him to the place Golgotha, which is translated, Place of a Skull.
verses.15:23: And they were giving Him wine mixed with myrrh to drink, and He did not accept it.
verses.15:24: And crucifying Him, they divided His garments, casting lots over them as to who would take what.
verses.15:25: Now it was the third hour, and they crucified Him.
verses.15:26: And the notice of His charge was inscribed: "King of the Jews."
verses.15:27: And along with Him they crucified two robbers, one on His right and the other on His left.
verses.15:29: And those passing by were blaspheming Him, shaking their heads and saying, "Aha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days,
verses.15:30: save Yourself, coming down from the cross!"
verses.15:31: In the same way, the chief priests also, mocking, were saying to one another along with the scribes, "Others He saved; He is not able to save Himself.
verses.15:32: Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe." And those who had been crucified with Him were reviling Him.
verses.15:33: And when the sixth hour had arrived, darkness came across the entire earth until the ninth hour.
verses.15:34: And at the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani?" which is translated, "My God, My God, why have You abandoned Me?"
verses.15:35: And some of those standing around, hearing this, were saying, "Look, He is calling Elijah."
verses.15:36: Then one man, running and filling a sponge with vinegar and putting it around a reed, was giving Him a drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah comes to take Him down."
verses.15:37: But Jesus, letting out a loud cry, breathed His last.
verses.15:38: And the veil of the temple was torn in two, from the top all the way down.
verses.15:39: Now the centurion, who was standing directly opposite, seeing that He had breathed His last while crying out in this manner, said, "Truly this man was the Son of God."
verses.15:40: Now there were also women watching from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joseph, and Salome;
verses.15:41: and when He was in Galilee, they used to follow Him and serve Him; and there were many other women who had gone up together with Him to Jerusalem.
verses.15:42: And when evening had already come (because it was the Preparation, which is the day before the Sabbath),
verses.15:43: Joseph of Arimathea came, a distinguished councilor who himself was also awaiting the kingdom of God, and he boldly went in to Pilate and requested the body of Jesus.
verses.15:44: Now Pilate wondered whether He had already passed away; and having summoned the centurion, he questioned him whether He was already dead.
verses.15:45: And when he had learned this from the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph.
verses.15:46: Then Joseph, having purchased a linen cloth and taking Him down, wrapped Him in the linen cloth and laid Him in a tomb that had been cut out of rock, and rolled a stone to the entrance of the tomb.
verses.15:47: Now Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph were watching where He was laid.
verses.16:1: And when the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus.
verses.16:2: And very early in the morning on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb, when the sun had already risen.
verses.16:3: And they were saying to each other, "Who will roll back the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?"
verses.16:4: And looking up, they saw the stone rolled back. For indeed it was very large.
verses.16:5: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a bright white robe, and they were astounded.
verses.16:6: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You are seeking Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen; He is not here. Here is the place where they laid Him.
verses.16:7: But go, tell His disciples and Peter that He is going ahead of you into Galilee; there you will see Him, just as He said to you."
verses.16:8: And going out, they fled from the tomb, for trembling and terror had overtaken them; and they told no one anything, for they were afraid.
verses.16:9: Now rising early in the morning on the first day of the week, He appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom He had driven out seven demons.
verses.16:10: She went and brought word to those who had been with Him, as they were mourning and weeping.
verses.16:11: And hearing that He was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe.
verses.16:12: After these things, He was manifested in a different form to two of them as they were walking, going into the countryside;
verses.16:13: and they went and brought word to the rest, nor did they believe them.
verses.16:14: Finally, He appeared to those eleven as they were reclining at table, and He reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen that He had risen.
verses.16:15: And He said to them, "Going into the entire world, preach the Gospel to every creature.
verses.16:16: The one who believes and is baptized will be saved, but the one who does not believe will be condemned.
verses.16:17: And these signs will follow those who believe: in My name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues;
verses.16:18: they will take up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well."
verses.16:19: And indeed the Lord Jesus, after He had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.
verses.16:20: They, however, set out and preached everywhere, the Lord working alongside them and confirming the word with the signs that followed.

notes.1:10: The Clementine Vulgate reads "cælos apertos" ("the heavens opened") rather than "torn open," and includes "et manentem in ipso" ("and remaining in Him," or "on Him"), an addition echoing John 1:32 absent from standard Greek manuscripts of Mark 1:10.
notes.1:13: The Vulgate includes "et quadraginta noctibus" ("and forty nights"), paralleling Matthew 4:2, whereas most Greek manuscripts of Mark 1:13 mention only forty days.
notes.1:27: Following the Vulgate wording and clause division ("quænam doctrina hæc nova? quia in potestate..."), "with authority" modifies "He commands" rather than "new teaching."
notes.1:38: The Vulgate splits the Greek compound for "market-towns" into two nouns, "vicos, et civitates" ("villages and cities"), and reads "veni" ("I came") rather than "I came out."
notes.1:44: The Clementine Vulgate reads "principi sacerdotum" ("to the chief priest," or "high priest"), whereas Greek manuscripts read simply "to the priest."
notes.2:16: The Clementine Vulgate reads 'scribæ et pharisæi' ("the scribes and the Pharisees") rather than "the scribes of the Pharisees" found in many Greek manuscripts, and also includes "and drinks" and "your Teacher."
notes.2:19: Literally 'filii nuptiarum' ("sons of the wedding"), a Semitic idiom referring to the wedding guests or attendants of the bridegroom.
notes.2:20: The Vulgate reads plural 'in illis diebus' ("in those days"), whereas most critical Greek texts read the singular "on that day."
notes.2:23: The Clementine Vulgate distinctively reads 'iterum Dominus' ("again ... the Lord"), adding "again" and naming the Lord explicitly where the Greek text uses only a pronoun.
notes.2:26: The reference to Abiathar as high priest is a well-known historical crux, since 1 Samuel 21 names his father Ahimelech during David's flight; 'panes propositionis' literally denotes the "loaves of presentation" set before God.
notes.3:5: The Vulgate distinctively reads 'cæcitate cordis eorum' ("the blindness of their heart") rather than "hardness of heart" as in most Greek-based translations.
notes.3:12: In the Clementine Vulgate, 'Tu es Filius Dei' ("You are the Son of God") begins verse 12 rather than closing verse 11 as in standard Greek verse numbering.
notes.3:15: The Vulgate includes 'curandi infirmitates' ("to heal illnesses") alongside authority to drive out demons, a longer reading omitted in many critical Greek editions.
notes.3:18: 'Cananæum' ("Cananaean") transliterates the Aramaic epithet meaning "zealous one" (cf. "Zealot" in Luke 6:15) rather than indicating a native of Canaan.
notes.3:22: The Vulgate preserves the name in its Latin form 'Beelzebub' (reflecting the Old Testament name in 2 Kings 1:2) rather than the Greek form Beelzeboul.
notes.4:10: The Vulgate reads hi qui cum eo erant duodecim ("those who were with Him, the twelve") without a preposition separating two groups, and has singular parabolam ("the parable") where critical Greek texts read plural "the parables."
notes.4:12: The Vulgate repeats the verb video three times (videntes videant, et non videant) and includes peccata ("sins") at the end of the verse, whereas modern critical Greek editions distinguish seeing from perceiving and omit "sins."
notes.4:27: The Vulgate reads dum nescit ille ("while he does not know") with temporal dum, rather than Greek hos ("how he does not know").
notes.4:37: The Vulgate uses singular mittebat with procella ("storm") as subject throwing fluctus ("the waves") into the boat, and omits "already" before impleretur navis.
notes.4:41: In this Clementine Vulgate versification, the material divided as verses 40-41 in modern editions appears under verse 41; the Latin also includes parenthetical putas ("do you think") in the disciples' question and necdum ("not yet") in Jesus' rebuke.
notes.5:1: The Clementine Vulgate renders this phrase as "across the strait of the sea" (trans fretum maris; likewise "across the strait" in 5:21), where the Greek reads simply "to the other side of the sea."
notes.5:13: The Clementine Vulgate reads "with a great rush" (magno impetu) without the Greek reference to a "steep bank," and explicitly includes "immediately Jesus" (statim Jesus) in the opening clause.
notes.5:15: The Clementine Vulgate describes him simply as "the one who had been tormented by the demon" (illum qui a daemonio vexabatur), omitting the Greek appositive phrase "the one who had had the legion."
notes.5:34: Latin salvus/salva (rendered consistently as "saved" in 5:23, 5:28, and 5:34) spans both physical deliverance/restoration and spiritual salvation, contrasted here with sana ("healed" / "sound").
notes.5:36: The Clementine Vulgate reads "having heard the word" (audito verbo), following the Greek variant akousas rather than the critical Greek reading parakousas ("overhearing" or "ignoring").
notes.6:3: Latin faber denotes a craftsman or artisan (traditionally rendered "carpenter"). The Vulgate reads Joseph (matching certain ancient manuscripts), whereas many Greek texts read "Joses."
notes.6:4: The Vulgate places "in his house" (in domo sua) before "among his relatives" (in cognatione sua), reversing the order found in most Greek manuscripts.
notes.6:20: Following the majority Greek tradition (polla epoiei), the Vulgate reads multa faciebat ("he did many things"), whereas critical Greek editions read polla eporei ("he was greatly perplexed").
notes.6:26: The Vulgate reads singular "the oath" (jusjurandum) and echoes contristatus est ("was grieved") with contristare ("to grieve her"), where the Greek has plural "oaths" and athetesai ("to refuse her").
notes.6:52: The Vulgate reads obcaecatum ("blinded"), whereas the Greek reads peporomene ("hardened").
notes.7:3: Latin crebro ("frequently") reflects the Greek variant pykna ("often"), whereas many Greek manuscripts read pygme ("with the fist" or "thoroughly").
notes.7:7: The Clementine Vulgate joins "doctrines and precepts of men" with et ("and"), whereas the Greek lacks "and" and is commonly rendered "teaching as doctrines the commandments of men."
notes.7:15: Latin communicant (also in vv. 18, 20, 23) literally means "make common," a biblical Latin calque for ritual defilement corresponding to "common hands" in vv. 2 and 5. The Clementine Vulgate omits v. 16.
notes.7:19: In the Clementine Vulgate, "cleansing all foods?" (purgans omnes escas?) stands within Jesus's question rather than as a parenthetical narrator comment (as in many modern translations of the Greek masculine participle katharizon).
notes.7:34: The Clementine Vulgate prints suscipiens in caelum, a well-known historical Vulgate variant for suspiciens ("looking up") to heaven; similarly, in v. 32 the Vulgate reads mutum ("mute") where the Greek has mogilalon ("having difficulty speaking").
notes.8:12: Latin literally reads "if a sign will be given to this generation" (si dabitur generationi isti signum), preserving a Semitic oath idiom that expresses an emphatic negative.
notes.8:17: The Clementine Vulgate has future cognoscetis ("Will you not yet perceive") alongside present intelligitis, and reads caecatum ("blinded") where the Greek text reads "hardened."
notes.8:25: The Vulgate reads et coepit videre ("and he began to see"), where critical Greek editions read "and he looked intently."
notes.8:26: The Vulgate preserves the fuller command "Go to your home, and if you enter the village, tell no one," whereas critical Greek editions read simply "Do not even enter the village."
notes.8:35: Latin anima, rendered "life" here and "soul" in verses 36-37, encompasses both earthly life and the enduring soul.
notes.9:10: The Vulgate renders the disciples' question with a temporal clause ("quid esset, cum a mortuis resurrexerit"), echoing Jesus's exact words in 9:9, rather than an infinitive ("what rising from the dead meant").
notes.9:11: The Vulgate reads "pharisæi et scribæ" ("the Pharisees and scribes"), whereas the Greek textual tradition mentions only "the scribes."
notes.9:12: The Clementine Vulgate ends this verse with a period rather than a question mark, though "et quomodo" ("and how") renders the Greek interrogative and contrasts with "sicut" ("just as") in 9:13.
notes.9:15: The Vulgate translates the crowd's reaction with two verbs ("stupefactus est, et expaverunt," "were astounded and struck with fear") where the Greek has a single verb.
notes.9:29: Following the broader Latin and Byzantine tradition, the Vulgate includes "et jejunio" ("and fasting") alongside prayer; likewise, it retains "credere" ("to believe") in 9:23, "in vitam æternam" ("into eternal life") and "ignis inextinguibilis" ("of unquenchable fire") in 9:45, and "et omnis victima sale salietur" ("and every sacrifice will be salted with salt") in 9:49.
notes.10:7: The Clementine Vulgate includes "and will cling to his wife" (et adhærebit ad uxorem suam), a clause omitted in several early Greek manuscripts.
notes.10:19: The Clementine Vulgate places "do not commit adultery" (ne adulteres) before "do not kill" (ne occidas), reversing the order found in most Greek manuscripts of Mark.
notes.10:24: The Clementine Vulgate includes "for those who trust in riches" (confidentes in pecuniis), reflecting the longer Byzantine textual tradition rather than the shorter Alexandrian Greek text.
notes.10:33: The Clementine Vulgate adds "and to the elders" (et senioribus) to the chief priests and scribes, a distinctive reading absent from most Greek witnesses.
notes.10:40: The Clementine Vulgate includes "to you" (vobis) in "is not Mine to give to you," whereas most critical Greek editions omit the pronoun.
notes.11:1: The Vulgate reads "Jerusalem and Bethany" (Jerosolymæ et Bethaniæ), omitting Bethphage, which appears in most Greek manuscripts.
notes.11:19: The Vulgate uses the singular verb egrediebatur ("He went out"), whereas many critical Greek texts read the plural ("they went out").
notes.11:24: The Vulgate reads the future accipietis ("you will receive"), whereas the earliest Greek manuscripts read the aorist ("you have received").
notes.11:25: The Latin text reads si quis habetis (a textual variant for si quid habetis, "if you hold anything") and peccata ("sins," where the Greek has "trespasses").
notes.11:32: The Vulgate reads the first-person timemus populum ("we fear the people") as part of the leaders' direct speech, whereas most Greek manuscripts shift to third-person narration ("they feared the crowd").
notes.12:14: The Clementine Vulgate compresses the closing question into a single clause ("or shall we not give it?"), whereas Greek manuscripts read "or not? Shall we give, or shall we not give?"
notes.12:15: Latin "versutiam" ("craftiness") is a distinctly Vulgate lexical choice here, where Greek manuscripts read "hypocrisy."
notes.12:29: The Vulgate reads "the Lord your God is one God" ("Dominus Deus tuus, Deus unus est"), echoing Deuteronomy 6:4, whereas Greek manuscripts read "the Lord our God, the Lord is one."
notes.12:33: The Vulgate lists all four faculties, including "and with the entire soul" ("et ex tota anima"), where critical Greek editions omit "soul," and moves from passive ("ut diligatur," "for Him to be loved") to active ("diligere," "to love").
notes.12:42: Latin "minuta" refers to tiny copper coins (Greek "lepta"), and a "quadrans" was the smallest Roman bronze coin, valued at one quarter of an as.
notes.13:5: The Clementine Vulgate reads the neuter pronoun quid ("anything" / "nothing") rather than the masculine quis ("anyone"), broadening the warning beyond human deceivers to anything that might mislead.
notes.13:19: The Vulgate uses the plural predicate nominative tribulationes tales ("tribulations such as..."), directly equating those days with the tribulations themselves, where the Greek text uses a singular noun.
notes.13:25: The Vulgate reads the genitive stellae caeli ("the stars of heaven") with the periphrastic erunt decidentes ("will be falling down"), rather than "falling from heaven" as in the Greek text.
notes.13:29: Latin sit has no expressed subject; it is rendered "He is near" (referring to the Son of Man of verse 26), though it may also be understood impersonally as "it is near" (referring to the end or fulfillment).
notes.13:34: The Vulgate joins cujusque operis ("of each task") as a genitive modifying potestatem ("authority"), rather than separating "authority" and "to each his work" as in the Greek text.
notes.14:3: The Vulgate reads nardi spicati ("spikenard," literally "spiked nard"), reflecting the traditional Latin rendering of the rare Greek adjective pistikes (often taken in modern Greek scholarship as "pure" or "genuine").
notes.14:14: Latin refectio literally means "refreshment" or "dining room/refectory," translating Greek katalyma ("guest room"). In 14:15 the Clementine Vulgate likewise describes the upper room solely as stratum ("furnished"), without a second word for "ready."
notes.14:24: Unlike modern critical Greek texts, the Clementine Vulgate includes novi ("new") with testamenti ("covenant/testament") and puts the verb in the future passive (effundetur, "will be poured out").
notes.14:27: The Clementine Vulgate includes in me in nocte ista ("because of Me on this night") here and in te ("because of You") in 14:29, preserving readings omitted in shorter critical Greek editions.
notes.14:45: The Clementine Vulgate includes the greeting Ave ("Greetings" or "Hail") before Rabbi, whereas Greek manuscripts read Rabbi once or twice without a preceding greeting.
notes.14:61: Here (Dei benedicti, "of the blessed God") and in 14:62 (virtutis Dei, "of the power of God"), the Clementine Vulgate explicitly includes Dei ("of God") where the Greek uses reverential circumlocutions ("the Blessed One" and "the Power") alone.
notes.14:72: The Vulgate renders the debated Greek participle epibalōn ("breaking down" or "thinking upon it") simply as cœpit ("he began to weep").
notes.15:7: Vulgate reads singular qui ... fecerat ("who had committed"), explicitly attributing the murder during the insurrection to Barabbas himself, whereas the Greek uses a plural verb referring to the insurgents generally.
notes.15:22: Latin Calvariae locus literally means "Place of a Skull" (from calvaria, "skull"), translating the Aramaic name Golgotha and giving rise to the English name "Calvary."
notes.15:27: Verse 28 ("And the Scripture was fulfilled which says, 'He was numbered with the transgressors'") is absent from the Clementine Vulgate, so the verse numbering passes directly from 15:27 to 15:29.
notes.15:29: Vulgate adds Dei ("the temple of God"), where most modern Greek editions read simply "the temple."
notes.15:40: Vulgate reads Joseph here and in 15:47 (literally Maria Joseph, "Mary [the mother] of Joseph"), where most Greek manuscripts read the shorter form Joses.
notes.16:1: Vulgate specifies Jesum ("Jesus") rather than a pronoun ("him") as in most Greek manuscripts.
notes.16:2: Latin una sabbatorum (literally "on one of the Sabbaths") is a Semitic idiom meaning "on the first day of the week" (compare prima sabbati in 16:9).
notes.16:8: Vulgate renders Greek ekstasis ("astonishment/bewilderment") with pavor ("terror/dread").
notes.16:19: Vulgate uses the present tense sedet ("sits") rather than the Greek aorist ("sat down"), emphasizing Christ's ongoing session at the right hand of God.
